title: [Proposal] Improve RAHP adoption with guided repository architecture, visual documentation, and specification pressure-testing workflow
body:
## Summary The RAHP repository is already developing into a strong and reusable risks-and-harms assurance toolkit. The main adoption barrier now appears to be **information architecture and discoverability**, rather than lack of substantive content. At present, a new contributor or standards author has to infer several important things: - which files define the portable RAHP method; - which files are the DTG-specific instance; - which files are canonical source data; - which outputs are generated; - how the artefacts relate to one another; - how RAHP should actually be used to pressure-test a specification; and - which findings belong in a specification versus governance, implementation guidance, runtime controls, or another layer. The repository would be easier to understand, adopt, and extend if it were reorganized around a **guided operating model**, supported by a small set of diagrams and a first-class specification pressure-testing workflow. This issue proposes an incremental path that should improve adoption without changing the underlying RAHP method unnecessarily. ## Relevance The current repository contains substantial value: - risks; - controls; - guardrails; - assurance tests; - metrics; - personas; - scenarios; - recommendations; - governance precedents; and - supporting tooling. The challenge is that the repository presently behaves more like a **collection of assurance artefacts** than a **guided method that another Working Group can immediately apply**. For adoption, the first questions a new user is likely to ask are: 1. What is RAHP? 2. How do I use it on my specification? 3. What is DTG-specific versus portable? 4. How do I contribute new findings? 5. How do findings map to changes in a specification? 6. What belongs outside the specification? The repository should make those answers obvious within the first few minutes. # 1. Align the repository layout with the architecture already implied by the documentation and tooling The README and contribution guidance describe a separation between: - `method/` - `data/` - `tools/` - `context/` - `build/` That separation is useful and should become the actual repository structure. The present archive still places canonical YAML, tooling, generated output, legacy documents, spreadsheets, and web artefacts close together. This makes it difficult for a newcomer to know what should be read, edited, generated, or ignored. ## Proposed repository structure ```text dtgwg-rahp-tf/ │ ├── README.md ├── QUICKSTART.md ├── ADOPTION.md ├── CONTRIBUTING.md ├── CHANGELOG.md ├── ROADMAP.md │ ├── docs/ │ ├── index.md │ ├── concepts.md │ ├── how-rahp-works.md │ ├── pressure-testing-a-spec.md │ ├── interpreting-results.md │ ├── governance-boundaries.md │ └── diagrams/ │ ├── repository-map.md │ ├── lifecycle.md │ └── artefact-relationships.md │ ├── method/ │ ├── lifecycle.yaml │ ├── vocabularies.yaml │ └── schema/ │ └── rahp.schema.json │ ├── data/ │ ├── instance.yaml │ ├── risks.yaml │ ├── controls.yaml │ ├── guardrails.yaml │ ├── assurance-tests.yaml │ ├── metrics.yaml │ ├── personas.yaml │ ├── user-stories.yaml │ ├── scenarios.yaml │ ├── epics.yaml │ ├── recommendations.yaml │ ├── risk-acceptances.yaml │ └── governance-precedents.yaml │ ├── examples/ │ ├── dtg-credential-spec/ │ │ ├── README.md │ │ └── pressure-test.md │ └── minimal-instance/ │ └── ... │ ├── tools/ │ ├── build.py │ ├── validate.py │ └── import_xlsx.py │ ├── context/ │ └── rahp.jsonld │ ├── build/ │ └── ... │ └── archive/ ├── legacy-spreadsheets/ └── legacy-documents/ ``` ## Why this helps This makes four distinctions immediately visible: - **method** = portable RAHP mechanics; - **data** = a concrete RAHP instance; - **tools** = validation/build automation; - **build** = generated output. The `examples/` directory then becomes the bridge between theory and use. # 2. Add a full repository map to the README A repository diagram would make the operating model understandable much faster than prose alone. The diagram should show meaning and information flow, not only folder names. ```mermaid flowchart TB USER["Standards WG / Spec Author / Reviewer"] subgraph METHOD["Portable RAHP Method"] LC["Lifecycle"] VOC["Controlled vocabularies"] SCH["Schemas & invariants"] end subgraph INSTANCE["RAHP Instance"] P["Personas"] US["User Stories"] SC["Scenarios"] RK["Risks"] CT["Controls"] GR["Guardrails"] AT["Assurance Tests"] M["Metrics"] REC["Recommendations"] RA["Risk Acceptances"] GP["Governance Precedents"] end subgraph TOOLING["Tooling"] VAL["Validator"] BUILD["Build system"] end subgraph OUTPUTS["Generated Views"] SITE["Human-readable site"] NORM["Standards action set"] JSON["JSON / JSON-LD"] MATRIX["Coverage & cross-reference views"] end SPEC["Target Specification"] USER --> METHOD METHOD --> INSTANCE SPEC --> P SPEC --> RK P --> US P --> SC US --> RK SC --> RK RK --> CT RK --> GR CT --> M GR --> AT RK --> REC CT --> REC GR --> REC RK --> RA RK --> GP INSTANCE --> VAL METHOD --> VAL INSTANCE --> BUILD METHOD --> BUILD VAL -->|"integrity / conformance"| INSTANCE BUILD --> SITE BUILD --> NORM BUILD --> JSON BUILD --> MATRIX REC --> SPEC ``` ## Core message conveyed by the diagram The intended mental model becomes: > **People and contexts surface scenarios; scenarios surface risks; risks drive controls and guardrails; guardrails become testable; findings feed back into specification development.** # 3. Make “pressure-testing a specification” a first-class RAHP workflow A strong use case for RAHP is not merely maintaining a risk register. It is using that risk corpus to pressure-test standards and specifications. ## Proposed workflow ```mermaid flowchart LR A["1. Select specification
or change set"] B["2. Establish affected
personas & contexts"] C["3. Test against existing
risk hypotheses"] D["4. Identify new or
changed harms"] E["5. Map controls,
guardrails & evidence"] F["6. Determine specification
vs governance boundary"] G["7. Produce actionable
recommendations"] H["8. Feed decisions back
into RAHP"] A --> B --> C --> D --> E --> F --> G --> H H -. new evidence .-> C ``` ## Suggested documentation Add: ```text docs/pressure-testing-a-spec.md ``` This should explain: 1. how to select a target; 2. how to identify impacted personas and scenarios; 3. how to reuse existing RAHP risks before creating new ones; 4. how to identify harmful inferences or missing assurance semantics; 5. how to map findings to controls; 6. how to decide where remediation belongs; 7. how to record disposition; and 8. how to re-run the pressure test after a specification changes. # 4. Introduce a first-class “spec review / pressure test” record Pressure testing should ideally become reproducible and traceable. A minimal record could look like this: ```yaml review: id: SR-001 target: repository: trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec version: WD-01 commit: abc123 reviewed_against: rahp_version: v0.3 findings: - finding: F-001 risks: [RK-CR01, RK-CR02] disposition: specification status: open - finding: F-002 risks: [RK-SC02] disposition: resolved-by-pr reference: trustoverip/dtgwg-cred-spec#12 ``` ## Why this is useful This would allow RAHP to track: - what was reviewed; - which RAHP version was used; - what risks were triggered; - what specification version was assessed; - whether findings remain open; - whether a PR or later revision resolves a finding; and - whether a future version should be re-tested. This moves RAHP from a static risk corpus toward **continuous standards assurance**. # 5. Add a disposition model so every finding has a control plane One of the most useful lessons from specification pressure testing is that a valid risk does **not** imply that its mitigation belongs in the specification being reviewed. RAHP should make that distinction explicit. ## Proposed controlled vocabulary ```text specification companion-specification governance implementation-guidance runtime-control operational-policy out-of-scope risk-accepted already-addressed resolved-by-pr ``` A finding should carry one of these dispositions. ## Why this matters Without a disposition model, standards authors may interpret RAHP as: > “Here are all the risks; put all the controls into the standard.” That would make RAHP harder to adopt. The better model is: > “Here is the risk. Now identify the correct control plane.” ## Suggested diagram ```mermaid flowchart TB R["RAHP finding"] Q{"Where must the
risk be controlled?"} S["Core specification"] C["Companion protocol
or binding"] G["Governance framework"] I["Implementation guidance"] O["Operational/runtime
control"] A["Formal risk acceptance"] R --> Q Q --> S Q --> C Q --> G Q --> I Q --> O Q --> A ``` This diagram could be placed in both the README and the specification pressure-testing guide. # 6. Add an artefact relationship diagram and concise glossary There are many RAHP artefact types. Their individual meanings are understandable, but their relationships are not immediately obvious to a first-time reader. A concise conceptual model would help. ## Suggested definitions | Artefact | Plain-language meaning | |---|---| | **Persona** | Who may be affected | | **User Story** | What that participant is trying to achieve | | **Scenario** | What happens in a concrete context | | **Risk** | What can go wrong | | **Harm** | Who bears the consequence and how | | **Control** | What reduces likelihood or impact | | **Guardrail** | What must be true before progression | | **Assurance Test** | How a guardrail or control is proven | | **Metric** | How behaviour is observed over time | | **Recommendation** | What should change | | **Risk Acceptance** | Where residual risk is consciously accepted | | **Governance Precedent** | Existing governance practice that informs treatment | ## Suggested relationship view ```mermaid flowchart LR P["Persona"] U["User Story"] S["Scenario"] R["Risk"] H["Harm"] C["Control"] G["Guardrail"] A["Assurance Test"] M["Metric"] REC["Recommendation"] P --> U P --> S U --> S S --> R R --> H R --> C R --> G G --> A C --> M R --> REC C --> REC G --> REC ``` This could become the conceptual spine of `docs/concepts.md`. # 7. Add a “minimum viable RAHP” adoption mode The existing corpus is rich. That is a strength for DTG, but it can also appear intimidating to another Working Group. A new adopter should not think that using RAHP requires populating every artefact class immediately. ## Proposed minimum viable assessment ```text 1 specification scope 3–6 relevant personas 5–15 risk hypotheses controls only where necessary guardrails only for hard-stop conditions recommendations as the primary output ``` The repository should explicitly say: > **You do not need to populate the entire RAHP model in order to use RAHP.** A small `examples/minimal-instance/` would make this concrete. # 8. Add an adoption guide The existing technical guidance is useful, but adoption would benefit from a short practical sequence. Suggested `ADOPTION.md`: ## Step 1 — Establish context Identify: - the specification or system; - expected participants; - decision points; - trust assumptions; - power asymmetries; and - known governance constraints. ## Step 2 — Reuse before inventing Search existing RAHP personas, scenarios, risks, and controls before creating new records. ## Step 3 — Pressure-test Ask: - what can go wrong? - who is harmed? - what harmful inference can an implementation make? - what remains cryptographically valid but governance-invalid? - what assumptions fail under adversarial or exceptional conditions? ## Step 4 — Determine the correct layer Decide whether the mitigation belongs in: - the core specification; - a companion protocol; - governance; - implementation guidance; - runtime controls; or - operational policy. ## Step 5 — Publish actionable findings For each finding, capture: - finding; - impact/harm; - affected persona; - relevant RAHP risks; - relevant controls/guardrails; - suggested resolution; - disposition; and - status. # 9. Change the README entry point from “repository contents” to “what do you want to do?” The README should offer task-oriented navigation before detailed architecture. For example: ## What do you want to do? ### Review a specification for risks and harms Start with: **Pressure-testing a specification** ### Understand the RAHP method Start with: **How RAHP works** ### Explore the current DTG findings Start with: **DTG RAHP instance** ### Adopt RAHP for another Working Group Start with: **Adoption guide** ### Contribute risks, controls, or evidence Start with: **Contributing** This would reduce the amount of repository knowledge a new user needs before taking a useful action. # 10. Give the generated site a guided narrative The generated views are useful, but they are primarily database-oriented. A more adoptable site could expose three top-level paths: ## Understand ```text Why RAHP → people and power → risks and harms → controls and guardrails → assurance ``` ## Apply ```text Choose specification → pressure test → analyse findings → determine control layer → publish recommendations ``` ## Explore ```text Personas → scenarios → risks → controls → metrics ``` The existing generated risk/control/matrix pages can remain exactly where they are, but become drill-down views rather than the primary entry point. # 11. Move legacy artefacts out of the primary navigation path Older spreadsheets, Word documents, and generated artefacts remain valuable for provenance and migration history. They should be retained, but moved under something like: ```text archive/ ├── legacy-spreadsheets/ ├── legacy-documents/ └── historical-builds/ ``` with a clear notice: > Historical artefacts. Do not edit. Current canonical RAHP data is maintained under `data/`. This would make the repository root substantially easier to read. # What this proposal is not trying to do This proposal does **not** suggest: - changing the underlying RAHP risk methodology; - adding large numbers of new risks or controls; - requiring every adopter to use the full DTG corpus; - moving governance requirements into technical specifications; or - making the repository more complicated. The objective is the opposite: **make the existing work easier to understand, apply, and adopt**. # Expected impact The main benefit would be a shift in how RAHP is perceived. Instead of appearing primarily as: > a structured risk and controls repository, it could be understood as: > **a repeatable assurance process for pressure-testing standards against risks and human harms, tracing findings to controls and evidence, and feeding actionable changes back into specification development.** That framing is closer to what the repository is already capable of doing. The combination of: 1. a repository architecture diagram; 2. an artefact relationship diagram; 3. a pressure-test workflow; 4. a disposition model; and 5. a worked DTG Credential Specification example would make that operating model much easier for Working Group members, specification authors, reviewers, and future adopters to understand.

## Behavior

Addresses part of #9.

Add a small fictional membership-lifecycle exercise using the existing `rahp-spec-review/v1` contract. Two target documents are frozen in real immutable commits before the review records. The packet shows participant context, reused risks, source evidence versus interpretation, governance/specification control planes, structured resolution, a separately retained open finding and reassessment with the historical review preserved.

The governance finding closes only for documentary coverage after a fictional procedure is added. The renewal/interface finding remains open. No real authority acceptance, independent human review, deployment effectiveness or effective remedy is claimed.

## Scope and coordination

Eight paths: five training packet files, one contract-validation test, and ADOPTION/review navigation. No schema, vocabulary, canonical corpus, existing fixture, validator semantics or generated site changes. The corpus context is separately pinned in the companion guide because the existing review schema stores a method version label rather than a corpus commit.

This contribution is independently based on accepted upstream main `e3ad6648ebc8c1a9a625dbdbefc8ba68b5bbd1e0`. It uses #10's review contract and #11's adoption guide and does not need #12/#13/#14 implementation. Those decisions remain separate. The normal root validator/build gap is already addressed by pending #13; this PR does not claim that gap is solved on main.

## Validation

- Both new review records pass the existing CLI validator.
- All 12 tests on main plus this example pass, including existing negative cases and validation of the new records. If #13 is later merged, its three additional reproduction tests remain separately applicable.
- Local Markdown links, distinct pinned source/review identities, structured resolution and retention of the separate open finding checked.
- Actual source commits: version 1 `62c52b3f5b1768dcfc1f6fab598c8021f72e057c`; version 2 `9ab60bc285adeeeb8e2e743bda5b609736ad56b6`.
- GitHub-side diff inspected; three modular DCO-signed commits.
- No claim of active corpus CI on current main; #14 remains the separate pending CI contribution.

## Authority and provenance

Contributor-authored synthetic exercise, prepared with AI assistance. It is a teaching application of upstream contracts, not a copied downstream controller or a report about the DTG Credential Specification. The guide explains that SHA syntax and schema validity do not prove target existence, judgment correctness, decision authority or effectiveness.

No automatic cross-run lineage, new record types, releases, publication changes, auto-merge or contributor self-merge. Upstream maintainers decide acceptance and merge.

title: feat(vtc): the console explains itself, uses the full width, and Recognition lists every trust record
body:
Operator feedback on the Repos, repo detail, Recognition and Members pages: hard to tell what figures mean or whether anything needs doing, git-right records missing from Recognition, DIDs clipped, a third of a wide screen unused.

## Every page
- **Full width**: the 80rem `.content` cap is gone; prose keeps a readable measure (`.prose-measure`).
- **`InfoTip`**: an (i) that explains on hover, focus or tap — a real button with the text as its accessible description, so it works on touch and with a screen reader. Used on column headers, summary tiles, commit-trust steps, the guard, namespace rights and Recognition filters.
- **`DidText`**: an abbreviated DID that wraps at its colons instead of clipping, with Copy and **QR** buttons (`DidQrButton`, lazy-loads `qrcode`).
- **`SortableHeader`** and `lib/table-sort.ts` (lazy search + sort) are shared, moved out of Members.

## DID abbreviation (`shortenDid` / `vta_sdk::display_name::shorten_did`)
A `did:webvh` host longer than 12 characters with subdomains keeps its last two labels, so the path survives: `did:webvh:QmNvpxDbHu…:…storm.ws:glance-arrow`. Changed in both twins with their shared vectors; the console now asserts them too (`format.test.ts`), and `vta-mobile-core`'s copy is updated. pnm/cnm abbreviate the same way.

## Repos overview
- Namespace rights is a full-width table (right, holders with copy, Grant), each right explained; break-glass and departed-member cards sit side by side beneath it.
- The **VGI** column is now **Commit trust**, with a legend and four dot states — in place, missing, **not applicable** (dashed), failed — each dot titled with what the step is and why.

## Repo detail
- **Commit trust is answered first**: `commitTrustVerdict` gives "Enforced: only commits signed by authorized DIDs can merge … Nothing to do", "Action needed: …", or "Not enforced", then each step with its state and reason, the guard, and the latest check (whose failure is explained as usually a refusal doing its job). The bridge's raw step outcomes fold away.
- The summary tile shows that verdict and "2 of 2 steps in place · 2 not applicable" instead of "2/4"; every tile has an explanation.
- **Not applicable** (`bootstrapView`): the VTC stores each step as a bare flag, so a step outside the bridge's plan read as missing. It is now not applicable when the guard makes it unnecessary (workflow under the org required workflow or a bridge-posted check — design §9), or when the bridge reported it `skipped` or left it out of a run that reported others. A reported `failed` always wins. Recording not-applicable explicitly on the wire would be the sturdier fix; not attempted here.
- The registry section links to Recognition.

## Recognition — every trust record
- **Server**: `vtc/registry/records/list/0.1` now covers every record under the community's authority. `registry` enumerates `registry/record/query/0.1` by `authority_id` alone (new `TrustRegistryClient::list_all_trust_records`; membership-only `list_records`, which drift uses, unchanged). `local` adds the git-ns projection mirror to the membership mirror, rendered through the projector's own `Tuple::record`. Git rows: `recordType: "authorization"`, `authorized: true`. Filters apply to all rows; sort (entity, action, resource); the cursor is that triple, base64url JSON, and a foreign cursor is refused. No wire type changed.
- **UI**: reads every page, then search (name, DID, action, repository), Type / Action / Asserts filters, Clear, sortable columns, names beside DIDs, a per-row "only this DID" filter; a single authority is stated once instead of a column.

## Members

title: fix(repos): clone over gh's protocol by default, and warn when an HTTPS checkout cannot push
body:
## Problem
A Linux member cloned a community repository from the Repos view. Clones defaulted to HTTPS, but his gh is configured for SSH (`gh config get git_protocol` → `ssh`) and he has no HTTPS credential helper for github.com. Signing worked, but `git push` stopped at `Username for 'https://github.com':`.

## Change
- **The default protocol follows gh.** When a forge account (`f`) is chosen, it still decides the protocol: a gh token only works over HTTPS and an SSH key only over SSH. Without an account, an explicit `w` choice applies. Without either, openvtc uses `gh config get git_protocol -h <host>`, falling back to `gh config get git_protocol` (bounded at 5 s, R1.2). If gh is missing or gives no value, the clone uses HTTPS. The screen shows where the protocol came from, for example: `cloned over SSH (from your gh settings) — w to change`.
- The `w` form now cycles through **automatic / HTTPS / SSH**. Only an explicit choice is stored, as `clone_protocol`. Settings files from before 0.5 always wrote `"protocol"`, so a stored `"https"` is read as the old default. A stored `"ssh"` can only have been chosen, so it is kept as a choice.
- **A checkout that cannot push gets a warning.** The checkout view warns when all three of these hold:
  - the push remote (`origin`, or `fork` when `remote.pushDefault = fork`) is an `https://` URL on the forge;
  - `git config --get-urlmatch credential.helper https://<host>` finds no helper in any scope;
  - no gh account is chosen.

  The warning reads *git will ask for a username when you push: no credential helper for <host>.* The fix line offers `f` to choose an account, or the new **`R`** key, which switches `origin` and `fork` to `git@<host>:<owner>/<repo>.git`. New URLs are validated with `RepoCoords::parse` and passed as separate arguments: `git remote set-url -- <name> <url>`.
- **Before an HTTPS clone**, the not-cloned screen says when gh prefers SSH or when no helper exists. The clone's result note repeats the warning.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide)
- R1.2: each `gh config get` call is bounded at 5 s and the global `git config --get-urlmatch` at 10 s. Both run once per forge per open view.
- R6.4: each warning names its actual cause: no credential helper, or gh prefers SSH.
- R3.6: does not apply, because no service endpoints are added.

Tests and docs follow in later commits on this branch.

title: feat(repos): choose the forge account a repository clones, fetches and pushes with
body:
## What

A member can choose which forge account git uses for **clone, fetch and push** — per community and forge, with an optional per-repository override — instead of relying on the machine's default git credentials. "Use my different gh accounts for different repos locally."

In the Repos view, **`f`** opens a picker for the highlighted (or open) repository:

- **gh account** — every account `gh auth status` reports on that forge (gh 2.40+ multi-account).
- **SSH key** — the `id_*` private keys in `~/.ssh` (no `.pub`), or a typed path.
- **Git default** — today's behaviour; openvtc writes nothing.
- On a repository: **same as the community's choice** for that forge.

`Tab` switches between *this repository* and *every repository of this community on that forge*. `⏎` checks the choice (key file present; `gh auth token --user <login>` succeeds), stores it, and writes it into every located checkout it covers. If nothing is chosen yet and a forge account was linked this session, the gh account with the same login is preselected.

The checkout view shows `forge account: <label> (this repository's choice | this community's choice for github.com | nothing chosen)`, and calls out a checkout whose own config says otherwise (read back from its `--local` config).

## How it is applied

- **SSH key:** `core.sshCommand = ssh -i '<path>' -o IdentitiesOnly=yes` (openvtc's own clone also adds `BatchMode=yes` via a one-off `-c`).
- **gh account:** a credential helper scoped to `https://<forge>`:
  `!f() { test "$1" = get || exit 0; t=$(gh auth token --hostname <forge> --user <login>) || exit 1; echo username=<login>; echo "password=$t"; }; f`
  preceded by an empty `helper` entry that resets the helpers inherited from the global/system config. `gh auth git-credential` cannot be used: it always answers with the host's *active* account.
- **Clone:** `git clone --config k=v …` writes the settings into the new checkout before the first fetch, so the first clone already uses the chosen account; later fetches and pushes keep it.
- **Existing checkout:** `git config --local`, removing only what openvtc wrote for the previous choice (tracked by `openvtc.forgeCredential`).
- The credential decides the protocol: a gh account clones over HTTPS, an SSH key over SSH. A checkout whose `origin` uses the other protocol is called out.

Only references are stored (`git-workspace*.json`, `credentials.<vtc_did>.{forges,repos}`): a key path or a gh login — never a token or key material.

Untrusted-input rules: logins are held to GitHub's alphabet, key paths may not contain quotes or control characters (they end up inside shell strings git runs), hosts are already DNS names; every git/gh invocation uses argument vectors and keeps `--` before URLs and paths.

Verified by hand: the helper as written makes `git credential fill` answer with the named account while another gh account is active, and this very branch was pushed with it.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide)

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2) — `gh` calls are bounded (20 s) and killed on overrun; `git config` calls 10 s; clone keeps its 15 min bound
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1) — the choice is saved, then written into checkouts; a crash in between shows as "this checkout is set to …" and `f`, `⏎` re-applies (idempotent)
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4) — no retries
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] New/changed wire types (R3.*) — none; local settings file only, new fields `#[serde(default)]`
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*) — absent = git default, exactly today's behaviour
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; failures surfaced (R6.*) — "the key file … is missing", "gh is not installed", "gh has no account X logged in on github.com", "this gh cannot choose between accounts; update to 2.40+"
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1)
- [x] Deviations flagged: none



## Follow-ups from the live test (openvtc-plumbers/demo-repository)

- **The commit author follows the chosen gh account.** Pushing as `stormer78-2` still showed commits as `stormer78`, because the global `user.email` belongs to that account (and the commit was not *Verified*). Choosing a gh account now also sets the checkout's `user.name = <login>` and `user.email = <id>+<login>@users.noreply.<forge>` (id from `gh api users/<login>`, bounded). `a` in the picker keeps your own identity. Written and removed with the choice (`openvtc.forgeAuthor`); the checkout view shows `commits authored as: …`.
- **Per-repo account pinning without `gh auth switch`.** `gh auth git-credential` takes no user, so the helper runs `gh auth token --user <login>` (verified on gh 2.101 with two accounts on github.com). `useHttpPath` is not needed: the helper is scoped to `https://<forge>` and answers for any path there.
- **A cached keychain token never wins.** The `--local` config starts the forge's helper list with an empty entry, which resets helpers from the global/system config (`osxkeychain` included). Test `a_global_helper_is_not_consulted_for_a_chosen_account` puts a helper that answers with another account in the global config and checks it is never asked once an account is chosen. A URL-scoped reset is used (not a bare `credential.helper=`) so other hosts' helpers in the same checkout still work.
- **No push access is said, and `F` forks.** After a clone or a choice, `gh api repos/<o>/<r>` with *that account's* token reads `permissions.push` (verified live: stormer78 true, stormer78-2 false on both repos). When false, the screen says so; `F` runs `gh repo fork --remote --remote-name fork` in the checkout as that account and sets `remote.pushDefault = fork`, then says to open the PR from `<login>:<branch>`.
- **Linked-account mismatch is warned.** When the chosen gh account is not the account linked for this membership: "This membership is linked to X, not Y: pull requests from Y will be closed by the community unless it is linked — press l to link it." With no link known this session, a dim hint says the community accepts PRs only from a linked account.

CI note: the Coverage job fails in `git_signing_e2e` (`unsupportedType keys/sign-sshsig/0.1`), the same as on main since #475; fixed by #478.

title: fix(did-git-sign): use the credential store OpenVTC uses, so a Linux signer finds its credential
body:
On Linux the did-git-sign binary registered the kernel keyring (keyutils), but OpenVTC registers the DBus Secret Service through `vta_sdk::keyring_init::install_default_store()` and writes the signing credential through this crate into that store. So `did-git-sign -Y sign`, `enable` and `health` reported "has no credentials in the keyring" for a credential that was sitting one store over. The comment next to the old code said the two stores matched. That was true only until OpenVTC moved off keyutils, which it calls RAM-only. macOS (Keychain) and Windows (Credential Manager) already matched, so only Linux broke.

Seen live: OpenVTC's Repos panel showed the profile, the binary and the hook all green, and pressing `e` (sign here) failed in `include_for`.

**Change**
- A new `store` module picks the store the way OpenVTC does. By default that is vta-sdk's `install_default_store` (vta-sdk `keyring` feature). The module also honours OpenVTC's `OPENVTC_SECURE_STORE` override. `keyutils` on Linux selects the kernel keyring. `file` is refused with an explanation: OpenVTC's encrypted file store lives in openvtc-core, and it accepts only passphrase-encrypted profile blobs, so OpenVTC can't keep the signing credential there either.
- The direct apple/windows store dependencies are gone, since vta-sdk supplies them. keyutils stays on Linux for the override and for migration.
- The store is now installed after argument parsing, so `--help` and `--version` work on a host with no reachable store.

**Follow-up commits on this PR**
- Migration: a credential that an older did-git-sign left in the kernel keyring is read on a miss in the Secret Service, copied across, and logged once.
- Error text (R6.4): a missing credential names the store that was searched, such as "Secret Service (DBus)" or "kernel keyring". An unreachable store is reported separately from a missing entry.
- Unit tests for store selection and the fallback, using keyring-core's mock store.

Release: patch 0.18.2 on the vta-sdk 0.63 line, so OpenVTC can take it without moving to 0.64.

read on a miss in the Secret Service, copied across, and reported once,
so existing installs keep signing (until the next reboot would have
erased it anyway). Uninstall removes the kernel-keyring copy too.

title: fix(repos): admit git-ns replies at the inbound gate, so a TSP answer reaches the Repos view
body:
## Problem
A TSP-joined member's Repos view timed out after 30 s even though the VTC answered (`git-ns/view/0.4` status=200, no send WARN). The client debug log showed:

```
DEBUG openvtc_core::didcomm: unhandled message type — dropped typ=https://trusttasks.org/spec/git-ns/view/0.4#response
```

## Root cause
`OPENVTC_CATCH_ALL_PATTERN` (openvtc-core/src/didcomm.rs) is the gate `classify_inbound` applies before anything reaches `process_inbound_message`, and it had no `git-ns/*` arm. Over DIDComm the reply travels in the binding envelope and passes under the `trusttasks.org/binding/` arm, then `message_dispatch` opens it, which hid the gap. Over TSP, `tsp_document_to_message` opens the envelope *before* the gate, so the message is typed as the task (`git-ns/view/0.4#response`), matches nothing, and is dropped at `debug!`. `vtc/community/profile/show` worked because `spec/vtc/` is in the pattern. The test #474 added covers the classifier, not the gate.

## Fix
- Add `https://trusttasks.org/spec/git-ns/.*` to the gate. This covers every version and every git-ns task. `trust-task-error` and capability replies were already admitted.
- A message dropped at the gate now logs at **WARN** with its type, transport, sender and thread when it arrived over TSP or has any `trusttasks.org` type (R6.4). Mediator pickup-status heartbeats stay at debug.
- The census (`openvtc/tests/inbound_gate_census.rs`) now lists the git-ns reply types.
- A new test drives a TSP frame in the binding envelope through `tsp_document_to_message` and then `classify_inbound`, and asserts it is delivered as an `InboundMessage`.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide)
- R6.4: an inbound Trust Task that no handler claims is now visible at WARN.
- R3.6: the reply type was checked against the live VTC log (`git-ns/view/0.4`).

title: fix(vtc): the request log names the Trust Task, and a TSP request is logged at all
body:
## Why
OpenVTC's Repos view timed out for a member who joined over TSP. The VTC log had a single line from her, `message_type=…/binding/didcomm/0.1/envelope … status="ok(response)"`. From that line you cannot tell which Trust Task it was (a community-profile ask or a `git-ns/view`). A request that arrived over TSP left no log line at all, so it was not possible to tell which of her requests reached the VTC, or which transport they used.

The root cause was in the client: git-ns requests were sent over DIDComm, and the DIDComm reply never reached a persona that collects over TSP. It is fixed in OpenVTC/openvtc#474. This PR makes the same situation diagnosable from the VTC log.

## Change
- The `didcomm_server::request` log line now also records:
  - `task`: the type of the document the envelope carries;
  - `id`: the request id;
  - `reply_type`: the type of the reply, either `#response` or `trust-task-error`.
- `handle_tsp` now logs a `tsp_server::request` line with the task, the proven sender VID, the status and the latency.

No behaviour change. The VTC already answers a member's `git-ns/view` on both DIDComm and TSP, and a refusal goes back as a `trust-task-error` (`git_ns::tasks::handle_view_v4` → `respond`).

## Tests
- New: `messaging::tests::the_request_log_names_the_enveloped_task`.
- `cargo clippy -p vtc-service --all-targets -D warnings` is clean.
- The full `vtc-service` test suite is running in parallel with CI.

title: fix(repos,capabilities): send on the membership's transport, so a TSP-joined member gets its answer
body:
## Symptom
Member alice joined first-vtc over TSP. When she opens Communities → `r: repos`, the view waits 30 s and then shows "no reply within 30s — the community's VTC may be offline…". The VTC log shows her DIDComm binding envelope processed `ok(response)` at 05:20:10Z, but nothing arrived on the client. The community-profile ask sent alongside it over TSP got its answer straight away.

## Root cause
`openvtc/src/state_handler/repos_actions.rs` and `capability_actions.rs` both send through `capabilities::send_capability_document`, which only used DIDComm (`openvtc-core/src/capabilities.rs:85`).

Every other member verb already sends over TSP when the membership was joined over TSP: join, status poll, profile ask, VMC, leave, renew and personhood.

The VTC replies to a DIDComm request over DIDComm (`vtc-service/src/messaging.rs`, `handle_inbound_frame`). A persona that joined over TSP may not collect messages on that route, so the reply was lost.

The activity log does not show the reply, and that would be true even if it had arrived. The log records an inbound message only when it changes config, and a git-ns reply never changes config.

## Fix
- Add a new module, `openvtc_core::community_send`, with `Delivery`, `tsp_mediator_for(over_tsp, vtc)` and `send_document`.
  - If the membership was joined over TSP, it sends over TSP to the community's `#tsp` mediator, resolved fresh on each send.
  - Otherwise it sends the DIDComm binding envelope.
- Move `members::Delivery` and `members::send_document` into that module. Join and renewal now call it.
- `send_capability_document` now takes a `Delivery`. The repos and capability jobs carry the membership's transport.
- The DIDComm message id is now the document id, so the VTC's DIDComm `thid` equals the document's `threadId`.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide)
- R1.2: no new outbound client is added. Sends reuse the existing TSP and DIDComm paths with their timeouts.
- R1.4: no new polling.
- R3.6: request shapes and URIs are unchanged. Only the transport changes.
- R6.4: not changed in this PR. Follow-up commits cover the timeout wording.

## Follow-up commit
- `personhood::Route::send` and the three join, status and profile copies of the TSP-or-DIDComm choice now call `community_send::send_document`. All member-to-community sends now share one transport choice.
- The Repos timeout no longer says "may not serve git namespaces". A VTC that does not serve them answers with a refusal, which is shown in words, so a timeout can only mean the request or its answer was lost (R6.4).

## Tests
- `cargo test --workspace` passes locally, and `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -D warnings` is clean.
- New test: `didcomm::tsp_carriage_tests::a_tsp_git_ns_answer_reaches_the_repos_classifier_by_thread`. A `git-ns/view` `#response` or a `trust-task-error` that arrives over TSP in the binding envelope reaches the Repos classifier, keyed on the request's thread.
- Companion VTC log change: OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1982.

the repos and capability jobs now carry the membership's transport.

  TSP-or-DIDComm choice now call community_send::send_document, so there is
  one transport choice for every member-to-community send.
- The Repos view's timeout no longer suggests the community may not serve git
  namespaces. A VTC that does not answers with a refusal, shown in words, so a
  timeout means the request or its answer was lost (R6.4).

title: fix(git-signing): grant did-git-sign sign-sshsig, so the VTA signs and the key stays there
body:
openvtc granted each persona's did-git-sign credential `admin` of the
persona's context narrowed to `key-export`: did-git-sign fetched the key
on every commit. did-git-sign 0.17+ asks the VTA to sign instead
(keys/sign-sshsig) and, against a VTA serving that task, a `key-export`-only
credential is refused it — with did-git-sign 0.17/0.18.0 that stopped
signing outright (0.18.1 falls back to the export, with a warning).

The grant is now narrowed to `sign-sshsig` when the VTA serves
keys/sign-sshsig (asked with trust-task-discovery), and to `key-export`
only for an older VTA, which would refuse a capability it does not know.
The proof before anything is stored asks the VTA for a real SSHSIG
signature and checks it against the key the persona's DID document
publishes — the key is never fetched — falling back to the export check
for an older VTA or a credential granted before this change.

did-git-sign 0.15.1 -> 0.18.1 (still vta-sdk 0.63, one copy); openvtc-core
takes vgi-core 0.18.1 for the SSHSIG signed-data encoding.

Tests: `cargo test -p openvtc-core` (960 unit + integration, incl. `git_signing_e2e` against the published in-process VTA, which predates keys/sign-sshsig and so exercises the legacy path); `cargo clippy -p openvtc-core -p openvtc --all-targets -D warnings` clean. New unit tests: the grant is `sign-sshsig` only; an older VTA gets `key-export`.

title: fix(vtc): a grant holder's DID stays inside its column on the repos page
body:
On the repos overview, the *Namespace rights* card let a grant holder's DID run under the **Grant** button and past the card's edge once holders were added.

**Cause:** a holder with no known name renders as a bare `<code class="truncate">` DID. `.truncate` caps at `22rem`, which is wider than the holder column (`minmax(0, 1fr)`) in the three-up card row, so the column couldn't contain it. Holders with a name were already handled by the `.gitns-holder .named-did*` rules, which is why those rows rendered correctly.

**Fix:** inside `.gitns-holder`, `.truncate` is capped at `max-width: 100%` of the column, so it ellipsises like a named holder's DID. The `title` still shows the full DID on hover. CSS only; nothing changes outside the repos page's holder list.

title: fix(did-git-sign): auto falls back when the credential may not use keys/sign-sshsig
body:
`auto` fell back to exporting the key only when the VTA did not serve
keys/sign-sshsig (methodNotFound). A VTA that serves it answers a
credential holding neither `sign-sshsig` nor `sign` with permissionDenied,
and auto stopped there — so every credential openvtc provisioned (narrowed
to `key-export` alone, before the task existed) would stop signing commits
the moment its VTA was upgraded.

permissionDenied now comes back as RemoteSignature::NotPermitted: `auto`
warns, names the capability to grant, and signs with the exported key as
before; `vta` refuses with the same guidance.

Tests: `cargo test -p did-git-sign`, clippy clean.

title: fix(vetting): the vetter follows the request, and a new application takes up hidden vetting
body:
## Live failure

first-vtc publishes one vetting criterion, `vetted-member`, with `org.openvtc.hidden-vetting` in `vetting.ext` (VTC console: "On, alongside named vetters").

- **Applicant (alice):** the application showed `VETTERS NAMED`. Her request to devote-hotel carried no hidden-vetting identifier.
- **Vetter (devote-hotel):** the desk showed `PCS ZKP` and refused to attest: "this request carries no hidden-vetting identifier, so there is nobody to attest to under this community's criterion".

## Root cause

1. **Vetter:** the desk chose PCS vs named from the whole community (`hides_vetters`, which is true if any criterion publishes hidden parameters). The VTC publishes those parameters in `ext`, never in `extCritical` (vtc-service `manifest.rs`, §16), so a hidden criterion still accepts named statements. A named request was refused even though the criterion would have counted a named statement.
2. **Applicant:** `VettingBook::adopt_known_requirements` is how the join page and `n` start an application from the manifest already cached in the book. It copied the criterion's requirements but not its hidden-vetting parameters, so the application stayed `hidden: None`. `adopt_manifest` gets this right. A test against the live first-vtc manifest reproduces it.

## Fix (this commit; follow-ups below)

- `VettingBook::request_vetting(request_id)` decides per request:
  - a PCS identifier gets a PCS ZKP attestation;
  - no identifier, under a criterion that accepts named statements, gets a named statement;
  - no identifier, under a criterion that marks the namespace in `extCritical`, is refused. The message tells the vetter to ask the applicant to refresh requirements (m) and send a new request.

  The desk's PCS badge follows the request.
- `KnownCriterion::paths()` returns `Named`, `Either` or `HiddenOnly`, read the same way the VTC publishes them.
- `adopt_known_requirements` and `adopt_manifest` now share one `Application::adopt_criterion`, so both read the hidden parameters the same way. When a criterion offers both paths and nothing is under way, a new application defaults to hidden. An application that already has requests or evidence keeps its current path. Adopt failures are reported to the user instead of logged at debug only.

Follow-up commits on this PR:
- The application shows its criterion id, the criterion's description, its path (PCS ZKP or named), and how many ways the community offers to be vetted. A named application under a criterion that also accepts PCS ZKP explains why it is named.
- `p` on an application cycles criterion and path until any vetting is held. If a request was already sent, it tells the applicant to send the vetter a new request.
- A stale `criterion_id` is re-picked and the page says so.
- A ticket in a community offering both paths says that named requests get named statements. The token gate stays, because new applications default to PCS ZKP.
- Tests: the live first-vtc manifest, mixed-community default, switching before evidence, stale re-pick, per-request vetter decision (named, hidden, hidden-only refusal) and the refusal wording. CHANGELOG entry added.

Local: fmt, clippy -D warnings, test --workspace, test --no-default-features, rustdoc -D warnings all pass.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide)
- R1.2 / R1.4: no new network calls or polling.
- R6.4: the refusal names the cause (a hidden-only criterion and a missing identifier) and the next step. Adopt failures are shown, not logged at debug only.
- R3.6: the mode reading was checked against the current vtc-service manifest (`ext`, never `extCritical`) and the live first-vtc manifest, which is added as a fixture.

runs alongside named vetters - so a request without a hidden identifier is a

a PCS identifier gets a proof, none gets a named statement, and only a
criterion marking the namespace critical refuses, saying what the applicant
must do.

The applicant side had the other half: an application started from what the
book already knew (the join page's route) copied the criterion's
requirements but dropped its hidden-vetting parameters, so it stayed named
under a criterion that hides its vetters. Both routes now share one adopt,

title: fix(messaging)!: a receive leg that stops delivering is reconnected, and the SDK alone deletes frames we cannot unpack
body:
Adopts `affinidi-messaging-sdk` 0.33.2 and `affinidi-messaging-delivery` 0.1.20 (affinidi-tdk-rs #927) and wires the SDK's new receive-side controls into `vti_common::inbox` (#1978).

## Dependencies

- Workspace floors: `affinidi-messaging-sdk` `0.33.0` → `0.33.2`, `affinidi-messaging-delivery` `0.1` → `0.1.20`. `cargo update -p` moved only those two crates; no sibling TDK crate needed a bump (`affinidi-messaging-core` 0.1.11, `affinidi-messaging-didcomm` 0.15.10, `affinidi-tdk` 0.23.0 are unchanged).
- `cargo tree -d` shows no duplicate `affinidi-*` or `trust-tasks-*` crates.
- The delivery bump needs no wiring here. Its 10 s ack bound and 30 s slow-ack cooldown apply inside `MessagingService`.

## A receive leg that stops delivering is reconnected, within a bound

`run_inbox_watch` already saw this state: three status requests in a row unanswered while the socket reports connected. It now acts on it through a new `ReconnectGovernor` (R1.4):

- **Remedy:** `ATMProfile::reconnect_websocket()`. It re-authenticates, re-enables live delivery, and the mediator redelivers the inbox. The call is bounded to 10 s (R1.2) because it queues a command to the transport task. If the task does not take the command in that time, the task is wedged.
- **Rate:** at most one remedy per 5 min (`RECONNECT_MIN_INTERVAL`). While remedies do not restore delivery, the wait doubles up to 60 min, plus up to 10% jitter. Any answer from the mediator resets the backoff but not the 5 min floor, so a receive leg that dies again a minute after each reconnect is still reconnected only every 5 min.
- **Strikes:** a reconnected socket gets its own three strikes. If it is still dead after them, that is reported again.
- **vtc-service** (`Escalation::Never`): its session is published once in `state.didcomm` and cannot be rebuilt. Until now a dead receive leg there recovered only on the ~12-minute token-refresh reconnect. Now the VTC reconnects the socket about 90 s after the leg stops answering, then backs off as above. It never ends the session.
- **vta-service** (`Escalation::EndSession`): it used to end the whole session every time the alarm tripped, which meant a new ATM, re-authentication and republishing the bridge. That happened about every 90 s plus the supervisor's backoff for as long as the mediator was not delivering. Reconnecting is the better first step: it keeps the session, its published bridge and its in-memory TSP state. The VTA now reconnects first. Only when a reconnect has not restored delivery by the time the next remedy is due, or when the transport will not take the reconnect request, does it end the session for `MessagingConnect` to rebuild. The remedies after that alternate (reconnect, then rebuild) under the same backoff. The governor is owned by the supervisor's loop, so a rebuilt session inherits the backoff and does not start a fresh budget.
- **Overlap with the SDK probe:** the SDK's own probe (60 s idle, then 30 s to answer) will usually reconnect first. The watch is the second layer. It covers a socket that receives probe answers while status replies still go missing, and a transport that stops taking commands. Its reconnects are counted separately from the SDK's.
- **Error text (R6.4):** each failure is named by its class: no websocket transport for the profile, or a transport task that did not take the request within 10 s.

## `/diagnostics` → `inboxCollection`

`InboxHealth` gains:

- `reconnectsRequested`, `lastReconnectAt`, `nextReconnectNotBefore`: the watch's own reconnects.
- `receive`: a `ReceiveLegHealth` that mirrors the SDK's `ReceiveHealth` (`lastDataFrameAt`, `heldFrames`, `consumerStalledSince`, `probeOutstandingSince`, `probeReconnects`, `unprocessableDeleted`, `unprocessableRetained`). It is read from the SDK's `watch` when the snapshot is taken, so it is never staler than the SDK's last publish (R6.2). It is a mirror, not the SDK type, because it is a wire contract: it goes into `openapi.json` and `wire.ts`, and a field the SDK adds later must not change that contract silently.

`unprocessableDeleted` moves from `inboxCollection` to `inboxCollection.receive`, because deletion is now the SDK's job (see below). `openapi.json` and `wire.ts` are regenerated the way #1978 did it (`UPDATE_OPENAPI=1 cargo test -p vtc-service --test it openapi_snapshot`, then `npm run wire:generate`). The admin console does not read these fields yet.

vta-service has no equivalent surface. Its `/health` returns `{"status":"ok"}`, and the richer report is the `vta/health/details/0.1` Trust Task, whose shape belongs to the trust-tasks spec. The VTA's `InboxWatch` is updated the same way and is available for when such a surface exists.

## Who deletes a frame we cannot unpack: the SDK

Before this PR there were two owners. From 0.33.2, every SDK path that reports a frame on the unprocessable channel also decides whether to delete it:

- **Live DIDComm stream (new in 0.33.2):** frames with bad bytes are deleted at once. Policy rejections are deleted per `purge_policy_rejected`. Transient failures are deleted only after three failures over at least an hour. A `SecretsError` (our own key missing) is **never** deleted.
- **Pickup drain:** same rule as before.
- **TSP adapter:** same rule as before.

`run_unprocessable_quarantine` deleted every one of those frames on its second sighting, a minute or so apart. That meant a second deletion of a frame the SDK had already deleted, and, worse, a deletion of exactly the frames the SDK keeps on purpose: a `SecretsError` frame, and a transient failure after one minute rather than one hour. The SDK is the better owner. It classifies the failure from the typed `ATMError`, which VTI only sees as a reason string. It is the layer that holds the frame. And its rule matches across the live stream, the drain and TSP.

So:

- `run_unprocessable_quarantine` is replaced by `run_unprocessable_report(rx, health)`, which only counts (`unprocessableSeen`). It is given no `ATM` or profile, so it cannot delete anything, `SecretsError` frames included. That is enforced by its signature, not only by a check.
- Both services set `.with_delete_unprocessable(true)` explicitly, with a comment, because they rely on it.
- Removed with the quarantine: `Sightings`, `describe_frame`, `frame_id` and `UNPROCESSABLE_DELETE_AFTER`. The SDK's own WARN names each frame's id, envelope, sender and error class.
- The vtc-service integration test (`inbox_collection`) now pins the new owner: three anoncrypt frames are counted by the VTC, deleted by the SDK on their first delivery (`receive.unprocessableDeleted`), and the mediator inbox ends empty.

## Breaking (vti-common)

`run_inbox_watch` takes an `Arc<ReconnectGovernor>` instead of `exit_when_not_delivering: bool`, `run_unprocessable_quarantine` and the frame-description helpers are gone, and `InboxHealth.unprocessable_deleted` is removed. The same applies to `vta_service::messaging::service::run_inbound_loop`, which takes the governor. Hence the `!`.

## Tests

New unit tests in `vti_common::inbox`:

- reconnect backoff floor, doubling and cap
- at most one reconnect per interval
- 12 h of a dead receive leg comes to fewer than 20 reconnects, with gaps that never shrink and stay within the jitter bound
- a reconnect that works resets the backoff but not the floor
- `Never` never ends the session
- `EndSession` alternates reconnect → rebuild → reconnect, and recovery resets that
- a reconnected socket earns new strikes
- `receive` is read live from the SDK's watch
- the serialised `inboxCollection` shape, including that `unprocessableDeleted` lives only under `receive`
- the unprocessable report only counts

## Checks run locally

Running in parallel with CI; results will be posted as a comment.

## Checklist (vti-stack-development-guide)

- R1.2: the `reconnect_websocket()` call is bounded to 10 s.
- R1.4: reconnects are capped, backed off exponentially with jitter, and limited to one per 5 min. Session rebuilds go through the same governor.
- R6.2: `receive` is re-read from the SDK's watch on every snapshot, so it is never a latch.

title: fix(vta): an admin session whose replies stop arriving is noticed and rebuilt
body:
## Why

On 2026-10-05 two OpenVTC admin VTA sessions stopped collecting their mediator inbox for an hour. Every request still reached the VTA, but its replies queued until the mediator's per-peer cap refused them all. OpenVTC noticed nothing: `device_presence` logged its failures at debug level.

This is the OpenVTC follow-up to VTI #1978. It ships on the **published vta-sdk 0.63.3**. OpenVTC cannot move to vta-sdk 0.64 (where #1978 lands as `VtaError::RepliesNotArriving` / `VtaClient::receive_health()`) until `did-git-sign` (VGI) releases on `vta-sdk ^0.64`. Every published did-git-sign is on `^0.63`, so moving now would put two vta-sdk copies in the graph. That VGI release is itself blocked on a `trql-client` (affinidi-trust-registry-rs) release on trust-tasks 0.27 / TDK 0.23.

## What changes

- **Detection (`openvtc-core/src/vta_receive_leg.rs`, new adapter).** Counts consecutive **reply timeouts** on the admin session, using the two shapes vta-sdk 0.63.3 returns:
  - `TspTransport("timed out waiting for the TSP reply …")`
  - `DidcommTransport("timeout waiting for DIDComm response")`

  Any reply resets the count, including a refusal the VTA sent back. A failure to send counts as neither a reply nor a timeout. The count is fed by:
  - device-presence registration, listing and heartbeat (a periodic probe)
  - the launch-time `list_contexts`
  - the probe on a rebuilt session

  Two in a row means "replies not arriving". The module mirrors the SDK's `ReceiveLegHealth` / `REPLY_TIMEOUT_BREAKER` field for field and carries a `TODO(vta-sdk 0.64)` naming the blocker, so switching later only touches this module.
- **Text (R6.4).** The state reads as its own: "Your VTA received the request, but its replies aren't reaching this app — its message inbox isn't being collected (N replies missed in a row). Reconnecting…". It never says "unreachable" or reports an auth failure. `vta_failure` also stops calling a single reply timeout "could not reach your VTA".
- **Visibility.** The VTA panel has a **Replies** row under Transport:
  - **Healthy:** last reply age, plus any replies missed.
  - **Stalled:** `NOT ARRIVING`, what recovery is doing, the next attempt and when, and the last reconnect error.
  - **After a reconnect:** "Reconnected … waiting for its first reply" until one arrives.

  Device registration, listing and heartbeat failures log at WARN every time (they were debug) and also show in the panel and activity log.
- **Recovery (`openvtc/src/state_handler/vta_recovery.rs`).** The admin session is rebuilt by closing the old session (10 s timeout) and opening a fresh one (60 s timeout), whose connect drains the inbox. A probe (45 s timeout) then checks that a reply comes back.
  - Backoff is capped, jittered and exponential: 5 s doubling to 5 min, ±20% (R1.4).
  - One rebuild runs at a time.
  - The schedule resets only once a reply arrives on the new session, so a session that reconnects and stalls again keeps backing off instead of looping.
  - The rebuilt client replaces `admin_vta` in the runtime loop and the State-A loop, and reaches the device-presence task through a `watch` channel. The supervisor is created before the State-A loop, so a rebuild still running when a first join completes lands in the runtime loop.

## Tests

- **New tests cover:**
  - the reply-timeout classification
  - the tracker (two timeouts trip it, a reply resets it, clones share one count)
  - the text mapping (the runtime text and `vta_failure`)
  - the backoff schedule (5, 10, 20, 40, 80, 160, 300, 300 s, jitter bounds, reset, no overflow)
  - a rebuild triggered by reply-timeout errors
  - no second rebuild while one is running
  - the backoff continuing after a reconnect that stalls again
  - the swap after a rebuild lands
  - the panel rendering, and presence failure/recovery reporting
- **Checks, all on published vta-sdk 0.63.3 with no `[patch]`:**
  - `cargo fmt --check`
  - `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings`
  - `cargo test --workspace`
  - `cargo test --workspace --no-default-features`
  - `RUSTDOCFLAGS="-D warnings" cargo doc --workspace --no-deps`
  - `cargo deny check`

## Pre-merge checklist

- [x] No new reqwest::Client::new() / bare fetch(); all clients have finite timeouts (R1.2). The rebuild's shutdown, connect and probe are each under `tokio::time::timeout`.
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3). The tracker's `std::sync::Mutex` is only taken after the call has returned.
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect, or the flow is resumable with an idempotency key (R2.1). Nothing is persisted; `admin_vta` is swapped only once a new session has connected.
- [x] Every retry is bounded + backed off; non-idempotent ops are not blind-retried (R1.4). Rebuilds are capped and jittered, single-flight, and reset on a reply. The only request re-sent is a read (`list_contexts`).
- [x] Accept/poll/listen loops survive transient errors (R1.5). A failed rebuild reschedules, and presence failures are reported without ending the loop.
- [x] Acks/deletes happen only after durable handoff (R1.6). N/A.
- [x] New/changed wire types: camelCase, deny_unknown_fields where security-relevant, schema registered, all consumers (incl. JS) updated (R3.*). N/A, no wire types.
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive; fail-closed if enforcement can't start (R5.*). N/A.
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified; background-job failures are surfaced (R6.*). "Reconnected" stays separate from "replies arriving" until a reply is seen. Presence failures are at WARN and shown in the panel.
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" answered for every mutation touched (R2.1). No persisted state; a rebuild that lands after exit shuts the orphaned session down.
- [x] Deviations from this guide flagged explicitly with rule numbers. Detection covers only the wrapped calls, not every admin call. That is the R6.4 gap the SDK's own counter (vta-sdk 0.64) closes; it is tracked by the `TODO(vta-sdk 0.64)` in `vta_receive_leg.rs`.

fix(vta): an admin session whose replies stop arriving is noticed and rebuilt (#469)

A session whose mediator inbox is not being collected still sends: the VTA
answers every request and the answers queue until the mediator's per-peer
cap refuses them. On 2026-10-05 two admin sessions sat like that for an hour
and nothing in OpenVTC said so; the device heartbeat failed at debug level.

- vta_receive_leg (new adapter): counts reply timeouts on the admin session
  (the TSP and DIDComm reply-timeout errors vta-sdk 0.63 returns), reset by
  any reply. Fed by device-presence registration/listing/heartbeat, the
  launch-time context fetch and the probe on a rebuilt session. Two in a row
  is "replies not arriving". It mirrors vta-sdk 0.64's ReceiveLegHealth /
  RepliesNotArriving (VTI #1978); TODO(vta-sdk 0.64) to switch once
  did-git-sign releases on that line (blocked on a trql-client release).
- The state reads as its own (R6.4): the request reached the VTA, its
  replies are not reaching this app. vta_failure no longer reports a single
  reply timeout as "could not reach your VTA".
- The VTA panel shows the receive leg (last reply, replies missed in a row,
  NOT ARRIVING and recovery progress). Device presence failures log at WARN
  and show in the panel.
- The admin session is rebuilt (old one closed, fresh one opened, which
  drains the inbox) on capped, jittered backoff: 5 s doubling to 5 min,
  +/-20% (R1.4). One rebuild runs at a time, every step has a timeout
  (R1.2), and the schedule resets only once a reply arrives on the new
  session. The new client replaces admin_vta in the runtime and State-A
  loops and reaches the presence task through a watch channel.

title: vta-service-v0.55.0
body:
### Fixed

- **messaging**: A node that stops collecting its inbox is noticed, and its peers stop paying for it ([#1978](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1978))

* fix(messaging)!: a node that stops collecting its inbox is noticed, and its peers stop paying for it

  A message waits in its recipient's mediator inbox until the recipient deletes
  it, and while it waits it counts against its sender's per-peer quota
  (`limits.queue.peer`, 50). On 2026-10-05 two OpenVTC admin sessions stopped
  collecting: 49 VTA replies queued for each, and every further reply was refused
  `503 e.p.limits.queue.peer` while the VTA logged a bare "failed to send TSP
  reply" every 30 s. Sends worked; nothing came back. This makes that state
  visible from both ends and stops the stack making it worse. It needs nothing
  from an unreleased affinidi-tdk-rs.

- **vtc**: Handle inbound messages concurrently, so a bind's bridge reply is read ([#1973](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1973))

The VTC's messaging loop awaited each inbound frame's handler before
  reading the next. An operation that arrives by messaging and then waits
  on a messaging reply therefore waited on itself: `cnm git namespace
  bind` over TSP sends the bridge a beginBind job and waits up to 30 s for
  the answer, which arrives on the same stream and is not read until the
  handler gives up. Observed live: the bridge answered in ~20 ms, the
  mediator relayed it in 0-1 ms, and the VTC read it 30.1 s after the
  request — "TSP reply had no waiter" — while cnm reported "the bridge did
  not answer". Any inline bridge job reached over DIDComm or TSP is hit the
  same way.

  The loop now spawns each frame's handler, bounded at 32 in flight, as
  the VTA's inbound loop has since the same defect was fixed there. Per-
  sender ordering is kept where TSP needs it (a relationship-control frame
  is a barrier for its sender's later traffic, Keyring VTI-43): SenderOrder
  moves from vta-service to vti-common so both nodes share it, and
  vta-service re-exports it at its old path.

  The reader is factored into run_inbound_loop so it can be tested: a
  handler that waits on a later frame completes (it hangs, and the test
  fails at its 5 s bound, with the loop made serial again), and an invite
  is still handled before its sender's following task.

body:
### Fixed

- **messaging**: A node that stops collecting its inbox is noticed, and its peers stop paying for it ([#1978](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1978))

* fix(messaging)!: a node that stops collecting its inbox is noticed, and its peers stop paying for it

  A message waits in its recipient's mediator inbox until the recipient deletes
  it, and while it waits it counts against its sender's per-peer quota
  (`limits.queue.peer`, 50). On 2026-10-05 two OpenVTC admin sessions stopped
  collecting: 49 VTA replies queued for each, and every further reply was refused
  `503 e.p.limits.queue.peer` while the VTA logged a bare "failed to send TSP
  reply" every 30 s. Sends worked; nothing came back. This makes that state
  visible from both ends and stops the stack making it worse. It needs nothing
  from an unreleased affinidi-tdk-rs.

- **vetting**: A new drip rate or live period no longer voids hidden-vetting attestations ([#1977](https://github.com/OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure/pull/1977))

requirementsDigest covered the whole hidden-vetting ext, so republishing how a
  community runs hidden vetting (dripPerTick, tickLength, vetter/token labels,
  events) moved the digest. A hidden vetter's attestation is bound to the digest,
  so every attestation in flight silently stopped counting: the proof verified
  and the join was decided request_more with nothing said. This held a live PCS
  join after the operator lowered the drip rate.

  requirements_digest now leaves those operational members out; the suite and
  keys stay covered, so an applicant still never binds to keys it was not shown.
  Label liveness is checked on its own when a proof is read.

title: fix(messaging)!: a node that stops collecting its inbox is noticed, and its peers stop paying for it
body:
## Problem

A message waits in its recipient's mediator inbox until the recipient deletes it, and while it waits it counts against its **sender's** per-peer quota (`limits.queue.peer`, 50 by default). On 2026-10-05 (mediator 0.37.0) two OpenVTC admin VTA sessions stopped collecting their inboxes. Each had 49 VTA replies waiting, the oldest an hour old, and every further reply was refused `503 e.p.limits.queue.peer`. The VTA logged `failed to send TSP reply` and `could not send a TSP relationship accept` about every 30 s. Sends were working and nothing was coming back. Nothing in the stack watched the receive leg end to end, and three behaviours made the backlog grow:

- The VTA had no inbox catch-up (the VTC has had one since VTI-50).
- Frames a node cannot unpack were never deleted. The SDK only reports them, so they sat in the inbox counting against their sender.
- vta-sdk's §7.2.2 D4 self-repair re-invited and resent after every reply timeout, with no limit across calls. Each call to a client that was not collecting queued two more replies.

The VTC's catch-up had problems of its own:
- **Unbounded (R1.4).** It re-asked for redelivery of an uncollectable backlog every 30 s, forever.
- **Logged at DEBUG only (R6.5).** A status request that went unanswered while connected, meaning the VTC was receiving nothing, never showed up at a visible log level.

The companion TDK PR is affinidi/affinidi-tdk-rs#927. It adds a receive-leg probe and reconnect, timeouts on the inbound chain, a bounded ack, and deletion of poison DIDComm frames in the SDK. **This PR depends on none of it** and builds against the released affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.33.

## Changes

**vti-common — new `inbox` module, shared by the VTA and the VTC**
- `run_inbox_watch`: the VTI-50 catch-up, now bounded.
  - Every 30 s it sends a status request. When something has waited longer than a live push takes, it asks the mediator to redeliver.
  - If the same oldest message is still there after a redelivery, the next redelivery request waits twice as long, up to 30 min, and the condition is reported once at WARN.
  - Three unanswered status requests in a row while the socket reports `Connected` mean the receive leg is dead. This is reported at WARN, and the session can optionally be ended.
- `InboxWatch` / `InboxHealth`: receive-leg health that is re-observed every check rather than latched (R6.2).
- `run_unprocessable_quarantine`: handles frames the SDK reports on its unprocessable channel.
  - On the first delivery the frame is reported and kept, because the failure may be transient and the catch-up is the retry.
  - On the second delivery it is deleted.
  - Each frame is named in a WARN with the sender the envelope claims (`skid`/`apu`, JWS `kid`, or plaintext `from`), the envelope kind, the type, the reason and the frame id. This is a deliberate R1.6 poison-message tradeoff, documented at the call site.
- `refused_recipient_not_collecting` classifies a refusal from the typed `QueueFullGate::Peer`; it does not match strings.
- `UncollectedPeers` logs one WARN per recipient, `{did} is not collecting its mediator inbox; replies to it are being dropped`, then logs at DEBUG for 5 min.

**vta-service**
- Runs the watch and the quarantine.
- When the receive leg is dead it ends the session, so `MessagingConnect` reconnects. The reconnect re-registers for live delivery and redelivers the stored inbox.
- TSP replies, relationship accepts and DIDComm replies refused per-peer now go through `UncollectedPeers`.
- An accept is not sent to a peer that was refused within the window. That peer re-invites after every reply timeout, so each accept was another refused send and another WARN.

**vtc-service**
- The catch-up now uses the shared, bounded watch, and the quarantine runs.
- Its TSP and DIDComm replies and accepts get the same per-peer handling as the VTA's.
- `/diagnostics` gains `inboxCollection`. The admin console's `openapi.json` and `wire.ts` are regenerated.

**vta-sdk (breaking: a new `VtaError` variant)**
- After `REPLY_TIMEOUT_BREAKER` (2) reply timeouts in a row, the D4 self-repair no longer re-forms the relationship or resends. It returns `VtaError::RepliesNotArriving { consecutive_timeouts }` ("the request was sent, but replies are not reaching this client … reconnect the session").
- Any reply closes the breaker. The breaker is shared by clones.
- `idempotency::is_transient` does not retry the new variant, and it has its own `suggested_fix` (R6.4).
- `VtaClient::receive_health() -> ReceiveLegHealth` exposes consecutive reply timeouts, time since the last reply, and time since the last timeout.

## Tests

- `vti-common` `inbox::tests` (18):
  - backoff never shrinks and reaches its cap;
  - a new backlog is asked for at once;
  - three unanswered requests mean not delivering, reported once per episode;
  - a request that was never sent is not evidence;
  - status-error classification;
  - frame description for authcrypt (`skid`/`apu`), anoncrypt, JWS, plaintext and garbage;
  - the sighting map is bounded;
  - per-peer refusal classification, including the sender gate being *not* matched;
  - one report per recipient per window.
- `vtc-service` IT `inbox_collection::an_unreadable_frame_is_deleted_on_its_second_delivery`:
  - runs the production listener on an embedded mediator;
  - three anoncrypted frames are reported on first delivery, deleted after the redelivery, and the mediator then reports an empty inbox;
  - **fails without the fix** (`unprocessable_seen: 6, unprocessable_deleted: 0`).
- e2e `inbox_collection::a_per_peer_refusal_is_recognised_as_the_recipient_not_collecting`: an embedded mediator with a per-peer cap of 3 and a recipient that never connects. It pins the classifier to the real mediator's `503` body.
- `vta-sdk` `client::receive_leg_tests` (7):
  - D4 still repairs one silent drop;
  - after 2 timeouts, the error is `RepliesNotArriving` and there are no further re-forms or resends;
  - a reply closes the breaker;
  - a keyed task is re-formed but not resent;
  - a transport failure does not count as a timeout;
  - the breaker is shared by clones;
  - the new variant is not transient.

CI-equivalent runs, all local:
- `cargo nextest run --workspace --exclude vtc-service --exclude vtc-client`: 5410 passed.
- `cargo nextest run -p vtc-service -p vtc-client`: 2864 passed after regenerating the OpenAPI snapshot.
- Workspace doctests pass.
- `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` is clean, as are the narrowed vta-service builds and `vtc-service --features vetting-pcs`.
- `cargo fmt --check` and `npm run wire:check` are clean.

## Follow-ups (depend on affinidi-tdk-rs#927 shipping as affinidi-messaging-sdk 0.33.2)

- Surface the SDK's `ReceiveHealth` beside `InboxHealth`.
- Have the VTC call `ATMProfile::reconnect_websocket()` when its watch reports `notDelivering`. Today the VTC reports this but does not tear down its set-once session. Recovery currently comes from the SDK's token-refresh reconnect, about 12 min, and from #927's probe.
- OpenVTC: show `RepliesNotArriving` as its own state in the VTA panel, and rebuild `admin_vta` with capped, jittered backoff when it appears.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide §9)

- [x] No new `reqwest::Client::new()` or bare fetch; every new await on the network is bounded. The status request has the SDK's 10 s bound, and the delete enqueue has a 5 s timeout (R1.2).
- [x] No lock held across a network await. `InboxWatch` and `UncollectedPeers` use short `std` mutex sections only (R1.3).
- [x] No local state committed before its remote effect (R2.1). N/A: health counters only.
- [x] Every retry is bounded and backed off. Redelivery doubles from 30 s to 30 min, and D4 now has a breaker across calls (R1.4).
- [x] Poll loops survive transient errors. The watch skips while disconnected, and a failed status request or redelivery is logged and retried on the next tick (R1.5).
- [x] Acks and deletes happen only after durable handoff — **flagged deviation**: unprocessable frames are deleted before handoff as a poison-message defence. The first failure is not treated as poison; the frame is deleted only on its second delivery, and the tradeoff is documented at the call site (R1.6).
- [x] New wire fields: `inboxCollection` in `/diagnostics` is camelCase and additive (outbound-only, so no `deny_unknown_fields`); `openapi.json` and `wire.ts` are regenerated. No new Trust Task URI (R3.*).
- [x] Config absence means the most restrictive behaviour (R5.*). N/A: no new config.
- [x] Logs and status claim only what was verified. "Not delivering" is reported only after the mediator failed to answer requests that were actually written to the socket. Background failures surface in `/diagnostics` (VTC) and through a session reconnect (VTA) (R6.*).
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" is answered for every mutation touched: in-memory health only, and frame deletion is idempotent at the mediator.
- [x] Deviations flagged: R1.6, above. The VTC does not reconnect itself yet (see Follow-ups).

title: fix(vetting): a new drip rate or live period no longer voids hidden-vetting attestations
body:
## Problem
`requirementsDigest` covered the entire `vetting.ext["org.openvtc.hidden-vetting"]` the VTC injects at serve time. Republishing **how** hidden vetting runs — `dripPerTick`, `tickLength`, `vetterLabels`, `tokenLabels`, `events` — therefore changed the digest. A hidden vetter's attestation binds the digest, so every attestation in flight stopped counting (`requirements-digest-mismatch`): the proof verified, the join was decided `request_more`, `superseded=false`, and nothing was logged. This held a live PCS ZKP join (first-vtc, 2026-10-05) after the operator changed the drip rate 100 → 20.

## Change
`vta_sdk::vetting::requirements::requirements_digest` leaves the operational members (`HIDDEN_VETTING_OPERATIONAL`) out of the hidden-vetting ext before digesting. **`suite`, `helperKey`, `tokenKey` stay covered** — `the_digest_covers_the_published_parameters` (keys) still holds, so an applicant never binds to keys it was not shown. Deny-list, so any parameter added later is covered by default. Label liveness is already checked independently when a proof is read (`token-label-not-live`, #1976).

The digest stays recomputable from the delivered criterion (both sides call the same function); OpenVTC only echoes the delivered digest, so no client change is needed.

## Upgrade note
Digests of existing **hidden** criteria change once on deploy (named criteria are unaffected); attestations made before the upgrade would need re-attesting — the same effect any parameter change had before, but now the last time.

## Spec impact
`requirementsDigest` is documented (docs/03-vtc/join-criteria.md) as covering everything about a criterion; the `org.openvtc.hidden-vetting` extension's operational members are now excluded. Doc line to follow if accepted.

## Tests
- vta-sdk: `operational_hidden_vetting_parameters_are_outside_the_digest` (drip, live period unchanged; keys, requirements change).
- vtc-service: `a_new_drip_rate_keeps_the_digest`; existing manifest/vetting/join suites with `vetting-pcs` pass (216 + 156).
- fmt, clippy -D warnings (vta-sdk, vtc-service + vetting-pcs).
